subject: sleep
title: Sleep: Two-Process Regulation and What's Still Unknown
summary: Homeostatic drive, circadian timing, metabolic links, and an honest open question.

cards.title: Essential and unexplained
cards.text: NINDS calls quality sleep as essential to survival as food and water, and also says its biological purpose "remains a mystery." What do we actually know about how it is regulated and what it does?

cards.title: Two processes
cards.text: Sleep-wake homeostasis tracks sleep need: the drive builds every hour awake and produces longer, deeper sleep after deprivation. Adenosine release promotes sleepiness, and caffeine counteracts it by blocking adenosine. The circadian system, set by the suprachiasmatic nucleus from light signals via the retina, times sleepiness and wakefulness across about 24 hours.
cards.example: Light is likely the single greatest external influence, which is why shift work and jet lag create a mismatch between the internal and external clocks.

cards.title: Architecture
cards.text: A night cycles through three non-REM stages and REM several times. Deep stage 3 dominates the first half; REM begins about 90 minutes in and lengthens toward morning. Memory consolidation most likely requires both. Recent findings suggest a "housekeeping" role in clearing toxins that build up while awake.

cards.title: Systemic effects
cards.text: In non-REM sleep, heart rate and blood pressure fall. Insufficient quality sleep is linked to higher levels of the hunger-regulating hormones leptin and ghrelin and to a reduced response to insulin. Chronic short or poor sleep raises the risk of high blood pressure, cardiovascular disease, diabetes, depression, and obesity.

cards.title: Dose
cards.text: Adults: 7 to 9 hours; adults sleeping under 7 may have more health issues. Teens 13 to 18: 8 to 10 hours. Children 6 to 12: 9 to 12 hours. NINDS adds that individual needs vary considerably at the same age.

cards.question: Sleep is the clearest case of an input everyone knows matters and almost everyone under-invests in. Why? What would change if you treated it like a scheduled operating commitment rather than a residual?
nudges: What is the real cost of the last hour of work at night vs. the first hour of sleep?
Which household "light and timing" levers are cheap to pull?

options.why: Correct. It masks homeostatic pressure rather than discharging it.
Light, not caffeine, is the main circadian input.

questions.q: When is deep (stage 3) non-REM sleep concentrated?

options.text: In longer periods during the first half of the night
options.why: Right. REM periods lengthen toward morning.

options.text: Only in the last hour before waking
options.why: REM, not deep sleep, grows later in the night.
It is part of normal nightly cycles.

questions.q: Which changes are linked to insufficient sleep, per NHLBI?

options.text: Higher hunger-hormone levels (leptin, ghrelin) and reduced insulin response
options.why: A plausible pathway between short sleep and metabolic risk.

options.text: Lower blood pressure during the day
options.why: Short sleep is linked to higher risk of high blood pressure.
The opposite: reduced response to insulin.
